body.text: Australia’s deterrence strategy is incomplete, because it pays no attention to a possible Chinese threat of nuclear escalation. The country needs to strengthen its coverage by the US nuclear umbrella to dissuade China from making such a threat.

Canberra’s policy of deterrence by denial aims to tell Beijing that a conventional campaign against the Australian continent’s northern approaches would be costly. It says nothing about what happens when the contest goes up the escalation ladder, and that is exactly where the region’s strongest military power is heading.

The numbers are moving in one direction. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s 2026 yearbook estimates that China’s nuclear stockpile reached about 620 warheads in January and will grow over the coming decade, with missiles loaded into vast new silo fields in the north of the country. Analysts at the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists reach a similar figure. Meanwhile, New START, the last treaty limiting American and Russian arsenals, expired in February, leaving no constraints on warhead numbers for the first time in half a century. The Indo-Pacific is entering a three-way nuclear competition with no rulebook.

In that environment, a purely conventional deterrent has a structural weakness. A nuclear-armed adversary can blunt conventional strength by threatening to escalate past it. If Australia’s long-range missiles hold Chinese forces at risk, Beijing’s answer need not be replying with conventional missiles; it can be the shadow of a nuclear weapon to which Australia has no matching response. Conventional strike that can be neutralised by nuclear coercion is not a deterrent.

Canberra’s safeguard has always been the US nuclear umbrella. The 2024 National Defence Strategy stated plainly that US extended nuclear deterrence was Australia’s best protection against nuclear escalation. That remains true, but extended deterrence is not a static guarantee. It is a relationship that must be renewed, demonstrated and shared. Australia’s contribution so far has been almost entirely passive: accept the umbrella, host joint facilities, say little.
Our regional allies are signalling that conventional strength and unspoken American promises are no longer enough.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has declined to rule out revisiting the principle that bars nuclear weapons from Japanese territory, while her defence minister has called for a debate without taboos. In South Korea, a poll taken in August after Washington abruptly scaled back joint military exercises found that 65 percent of respondents wanted their country to have its own nuclear weapons.
Australia need not seek its own bomb. But it should stop treating the nuclear dimension as somebody else’s business. It should take these three steps to turn a passive posture into an active one.

First, Australia needs a formal mechanism for coordinating deterrence strategies with allies. Both Japan and South Korea have one with the United States: the Extended Deterrence Dialogue and the Nuclear Consultative Group, respectively. Canberra should build one that, ideally, links these existing mechanisms and expands them into a wider Indo-Pacific consultation. This would give Australia a voice in planning for nuclear escalation scenarios that would directly affect it.

Second, Australia should make its geography count. Under AUKUS, up to four US submarines and one British submarine will operate for extended periods from Western Australia. US nuclear-capable bombers already rotate through northern airfields under a reading of the Rarotonga Treaty that bars stationing but permits visits. Rather than sheltering behind a policy of not asking or telling, Australia should openly support allied nuclear forces operating from its territory. Visible support is a signal; ambiguity is a vacuum.

Third, Canberra should protect the system that makes the American umbrella work. As I have argued elsewhere, US nuclear command, control and communications depend on facilities, such as Pine Gap and Naval Communication Station Harold E Holt, that could be attacked from submarines operating in Australia’s northern approaches. A conventional strike on them could blind or confuse allied nuclear decision-making in the opening hours of a crisis. Hardening and defending them is where Australia’s conventional investment and nuclear deterrence meet.

Critics will say this risks an arms race or tarnishes Australia’s non-proliferation credentials. But the arms race is already under way. The real question is whether Canberra shapes the region’s deterrence architecture or simply inherits it. At the 2025 Shangri-La Dialogue, Defence Minister Richard Marles called US extended nuclear deterrence a ‘critical if under-sung asset’ against proliferation. Under-sung is precisely the problem.

Holding the conventional card matters. Long-range missiles, submarines and an industry that can make guided munitions are all overdue. But as an adversary judges deterrence, it looks at the whole hand. If Australia shows only conventional strength, it invites rivals to play the one card it refuses to discuss. It is time Australia did talk about it.
